# Copilot instructions for rust/etw_helpers

Rust (edition 2024, MSRV 1.95) helper library for controlling and consuming Windows ETW (Event Tracing for Windows) sessions, built on the `windows-sys` crate (`Win32_System_Diagnostics_Etw`, plus `Win32_System_Threading`/`Win32_System_Performance` for the raw consumer).

## Build, test, lint

```powershell
cargo build                     # CI also builds on Linux (build only, no tests)
cargo test --features flume-async   # Windows only; what CI runs on windows-latest (flume isn't a default feature)
cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features
cargo fmt                       # run after making edits

# Single test (unit tests live in #[cfg(test)] mod tests inside each src file)
cargo test --lib consumer::crossbeam::tests::consume_event   # backend test modules keep their paths
cargo test --test sessions create_session   # integration tests in tests/sessions.rs

# Feature subsets (defaults = std + futures + crossbeam; flume, flume-async, hotpath and hotpath-alloc are opt-in)
cargo build --no-default-features --features crossbeam
cargo build --no-default-features   # no_std + alloc, raw consumer only (CI checks this)

# Profiling with hotpath-rs (see "Profiling" below)
cargo run --release --example profile_crossbeam --features hotpath
```

**Always run `cargo fmt` after making edits.**

Tests are real functional tests against live ETW: they register a `tracelogging_dynamic` provider, start a named file-mode session (usually with realtime delivery), write events, and consume them. They need rights to start ETW sessions (admin or Performance Log Users) and write `*.etl` files into the target directory (`CARGO_TARGET_DIR`, else `target`): build test file paths with `crate::test_util::etl_path(name)`. Each test uses a unique session name (`EtwConsumer-Rust-Tests-<Test>-<Backend>`), `.etl` file name and provider name (provider GUIDs are derived from the name) so tests can run in parallel—keep new ones unique too. Wait for a session to enable the provider with `crate::test_util::wait_until_enabled(&provider)`. **Consumer backend tests are shared** in `src/consumer/shared_tests.rs` (`#[cfg(test)]`): generic test functions over the public consumer traits, each taking the backend name and a constructor (e.g. `EtwEventWaiter::<B>::default` or `<EtwEventWaiter<B> as NewEventWaiter>::new_owned_events`), with fixtures (`RealtimeSession::start(test, backend)`, `write_events_to_file`, and an `observe` wrapper that reports `complete()` without touching backend internals). Each backend's `mod tests` instantiates them for its tag with `lent_waiter_tests!(crate::consumer::Tag, "Backend"[, extra_tests][; timed: extra_timed_tests])`, `owned_waiter_tests!`, `async_lent_waiter_tests!`, `async_owned_waiter_tests!` (including `into_stream`), `stream_tests!` (which also checks at compile time that `next()` futures are `Send`). Add behaviour tests there rather than per backend; keep only backend-specific tests in the backend module. A real-time trace only completes on its own when something stops it, so tests of "the trace stopped" use real-time sessions; file traces end by themselves (and report `S_OK` even when stopped early from the callback).

## Architecture

Two public modules: `controller` (`src/controller.rs` + `src/controller/`) and `consumer` (`src/consumer.rs` + `src/consumer/`). `lib.rs` only declares them (plus the private `error` and `profiling` modules) and re-exports `Error`/`hresult_from_win32`; don't re-export controller/consumer items at the crate root. Inside the crate, refer to items by their module path (`crate::consumer::EventRecord`, `crate::controller::SessionBuilder`).

- **Controller** (`controller/session.rs`, public as `etw_helpers::controller`): `SessionBuilder::new_buffering_mode` / `new_file_mode` return a typestate `EtwSessionBuilder<BufferingModeSession | FileModeSession>` (options valid only for one mode, e.g. `realtime_event_delivery`, live in mode-specific `impl` blocks). `start(recreate_existing)` calls `StartTraceW` and returns `ControlTraceHandle`, which **stops the session on Drop** (`manual_stop()` wraps it in `ManuallyDrop` to leave it running). `EventTraceProperties` is a `#[repr(C)]` struct that inlines 1024-u16 name buffers after `EVENT_TRACE_PROPERTIES`, as ETW requires; the byte offsets ETW needs are computed with `offset_of!` (don't hand-compute them). Sessions use paged memory unless `nonpaged_pool()` is called.
- **Consumer** (`consumer/processtrace.rs`, public as `etw_helpers::consumer`): `ProcessTraceHandle::from_session/from_file(name, processor)` calls `OpenTraceW`; `.process_trace()` spawns a thread running the blocking `ProcessTrace` and returns `ProcessTraceThread` (`stop_and_wait` joins it, `stop_and_get_thread`; closes the trace on Drop). Closing a real-time trace isn't synchronous; join the thread to wait for buffered events to drain. Anything implementing the `EventProcessor` trait (`fn on_event_raw(&EVENT_RECORD)`, `fn complete(err)`) receives events on that thread.
  - The callback context pointer is passed via `expose_provenance` / `with_exposed_provenance_mut`.
  - Panics must never cross into C. The callback is `extern "system"`, so a panic unwinding out of it aborts the process (Rust 1.81+); no `catch_unwind` is needed.
  - Returning `Err` from `on_event_raw` sets `stop_callbacks` and calls `CloseTrace`, ending processing.
  - After `ProcessTrace` returns, its result is recorded in `SharedThreadData` (read via `ProcessTraceThread::result`) **before** the processor is dropped, so once a consumer sees its channel disconnect ("ProcessTrace completed") the result is available. There are two ways to end a trace, both idempotent (the handle is swapped for `CLOSED_HANDLE`): `close_trace` only calls `CloseTrace`, so a real-time trace still delivers the events ETW already handed over; `cancel_trace` also sets `stop_callbacks` so the processor isn't called again (the callback's error path, `ProcessTraceThread`'s `Drop`, and `EventTrace`'s `cancel_on_false`). Requested stops (`EventTrace::stop`, `stop_and_wait`/`stop_and_get_thread`) use `stop_trace`: close for real-time sessions, but cancel for log files, since `CloseTrace` doesn't stop ProcessTrace from reading the rest of a file (`stop_file_trace` test). Tests that stop a real-time trace mid-way can't expect every written event: ETW buffers per CPU, and buffers not yet handed over are lost.
- **Public consumer types** (`consumer/backend.rs`): `EtwEventWaiter<B = Raw>` (lent), `EtwEventWaiterOwned<B = Raw>` (owned) and `EtwEventAsyncStream<B = DefaultStreamBackend>` (`Futures` if enabled, else `Flume`), generic over a backend tag: uninhabited enums `Raw` (always), `Crossbeam`, `Flume`, `Futures` (features), implementing the sealed `Backend` (and `StreamBackend` for streams). `imp::Backend`/`imp::StreamBackend` map each tag to its backend's internal types (`Lent`, `Owned`, `Stream`, `new_owned`); the public types wrap those and forward each sealed trait (`Connect`, `Wait`, `WaitAsync`, `Next`, `NextOwned`, `NextOwnedAsync`, `NextAsync`) with a `where B::Lent: Trait` bound, so which public traits a consumer has depends on its backend. The backend modules are private; never expose their types.
  - **Constructors:** `NewEventWaiter` (`new`, `new_owned_events(n)`, `new_with_timeout(t)`, `new_owned_events_with_timeout(n, t)`) is implemented for every `EtwEventWaiter<B>`, and `NewEventAsyncStream` (`new`, `new_with_timeout`) for every stream. Default type parameters don't drive inference, so a generic inherent `new()` would make a plain `EtwEventWaiter::new()` fail ("type annotations needed"); instead the *default* types (`impl EtwEventWaiter`, `impl EtwEventAsyncStream`) also have the same constructors as inherent methods, which win for `EtwEventWaiter::new()`, while a named backend (`EtwEventWaiter::<Crossbeam>::new()`) uses the trait (import it, or `consumer::prelude::*`, which re-exports every consumer trait). Inside the crate, call the trait explicitly (`<Self as NewEventWaiter>::new()`) to avoid recursing into the inherent method.
- **Consumer backends** (private modules, each a different strategy for bridging the ETW thread to user code; their types are `LentWaiter`, `OwnedWaiter` and `LentStream`):
  - `consumer/crossbeam.rs` / `consumer/flume.rs` / `consumer/raw.rs`: near-identical sync `LentWaiter` implementing `Next` and `Wait`. Changes to one usually need mirroring in the others.
   - `flume-async` (implies `flume`, enables `flume/async`) adds `futures-timer` and async impls for the flume waiters (`recv_async_timeout`/`with_timeout`, which only arms the timer if the receive isn't immediately ready), and `consumer/flume/stream.rs`, a `LentStream` (`EtwEventAsyncStream<Flume>`) with the same API as the futures one that reuses the flume waiter's `LentEvents`/`LentProcessor` (`recv_async` instead of `recv`). Async receives are cancel-safe: flume leaves an unreceived event with the blocked sender.
    - Each backend has a lent waiter (`LentWaiter`, `Default`: the callback blocks until each event is released) and an owned one (`OwnedWaiter`, `new(event_buffer_count)`: the callback copies each event into a queue of up to `n` and only blocks when it's full; events are always `EventRecord::Owned`). Each creates its channels in `default`/`new` and keeps its processor in `processor: Option<_>` until `EventConsumer::from_*` takes it (`sealed::Connect::take_processor`), so the receiving side always exists; before the trace starts, waiting simply times out. Waiters only report "ProcessTrace completed" (`E_TRACE_FINISHED`); `EventTrace` replaces that with ProcessTrace's result—never plumb the result through a backend.
    - Cancelling: `EventTrace` wraps every `wait_for_single_event*` closure in `cancel_on_false`, whose drop guard calls `cancel_trace` when the closure returns `false` **or panics**. That is what stops the trace in owned mode, since the processor may be idle with no callback left to notice. The owned waiter then marks itself `cancelled` and discards the queue (freeing a blocked send); it does this through `event_waiter::call_or_cancel`, a drop guard, so a panicking closure discards the queue too (and lent waiters likewise set `cancelled` after a panicking `Timeout` closure); later waits discard events until the channel disconnects (`drain`). Raw's processor still checks its shared `cancelled` flag, because nothing else would make it stop queueing after its waiter is dropped. Events queued before ProcessTrace completes are still delivered.
    - `consumer/raw.rs` has no channel crate dependency: it synchronizes with the crate's `Lock<T>` (`consumer/lock.rs`) over Win32 `SRWLOCK` + `CONDITION_VARIABLE`, with `QueryPerformanceCounter` deadlines. It only uses `core`, `alloc` and Win32 APIs—keep `std` out of it (outside its tests); the goal is `no_std` + `alloc` support. It is always compiled.
    - **`no_std`:** `lib.rs` is `#![cfg_attr(not(any(feature = "std", test)), no_std)]`, and every feature that needs `std` implies the `std` feature. Outside `std`-only modules, import `Box`/`Vec`/`Cow`/`ToOwned`/`ToString` from `alloc` and use `core` paths. The one remaining `std` dependency is the ProcessTrace thread in `consumer/processtrace.rs` (`extern crate std` for `std::thread`); removing it needs a Win32 thread, which changes `ProcessTraceThread::stop_and_get_thread`'s `JoinHandle`. For locking without `std`, use `consumer/lock.rs` (`Lock<T>`: an SRW lock + condition variable with QPC `Deadline`s, used behind an `Arc` by `raw.rs` and `SharedThreadData`).
  - `consumer/futures.rs` (`LentWaiter`/`OwnedWaiter`: implement the async sealed traits, and the blocking ones via `block_on`) and `consumer/futures/stream.rs` (`LentStream`: `sealed::NextAsync`; a `Mutex` + `Condvar` slot, no channels), behind the `Futures` tag. The waiter replies to the callback over one reusable `sync_channel(1)` with a `Reply` drop guard (so a panicking closure still releases the ETW thread), and `with_timeout` spins briefly (`spin_poll`) before going pending or arming a `futures_timer::Delay`, since both cost more than the handoff. Futures bounded channels hold `buffer + 1` per sender, so the futures `OwnedWaiter::new(n)` uses `n - 1` (0 behaves like 1).
- **`EventRecord<'a>`** (`consumer/event_record.rs`): enum over `Raw(&EVENT_RECORD)`, `Owned(EventRecordOwned)`, and `Serialized(EventRecordSerialized)`. `into_owned()` deep-copies user data and extended data out of the ETW buffer into an `EventRecord<'static>`; `EventRecordOwned` keeps the header and buffer context inline and everything else in **one** allocation (extended items in the serialized item layout, then user data). `serialize()`/`from_serialized()` convert to/from `TDH_SERIALIZED_EVENT_RECORD` bytes (tdhEx1.h; byte-compatible with `TdhEx1SerializeEventRecord`/`TdhEx1DeserializeEventRecord`: `Size, BufferContext, EventHeader`, 8-byte-padded extended item data, `Reserved1` preserved). `EventRecordSerialized` is opaque and can only be created by `from_serialized`, which validates once, so its accessors never re-validate or panic; its header and buffer context are returned as copies (`Cow::Owned`).

**Examples:** `examples/basic_sync.rs` (crossbeam: lent `next()`, owned `for` loop) and `examples/basic_async.rs` (futures: lending stream, owned `into_stream()`) are the commented introductory programs; they read `sample.etl` (not checked in) and exit with the open error if it's missing. Keep them simple and in step with API changes. The `profile_*` examples are hotpath workloads (see Profiling).

## Key conventions

- **Public consumer traits** (`consumer/event_waiter.rs`, re-exported from `consumer`): `EventConsumer` (sealed; blanket-implemented for every `sealed::Connect` type; provides `from_file`/`from_session(name, consumer) -> EventTrace<Self>`, called as `EventConsumer::from_file(name, consumer)`), `IntoEventStream` (`into_stream() -> impl futures::Stream`, gated on `futures`/`flume-async`), `EventWaiter` (`wait_for_single_event[_timeout]`), `EventWaiterAsync` (`wait_for_single_event_async[_timeout]`, returning `impl Future`), `EventIterator` (lending `next`) and `EventIteratorAsync` (lending async `next`; deliberately not `Iterator`/`futures::Stream`). All take `&mut self` (closures have no `Send`/`Sync` bound). Callers, examples and doctests must import the traits.
  - **Timeouts:** `*_timeout` closures take `EventOrTimeout<'_>` (`Event(EventRecord)` | `Timeout`); a timeout calls the closure with `Timeout` and returns `Ok` (only ProcessTrace completing is an error; there is no timeout error code). Each consumer can be created with a timeout (`new_with_timeout`/`new_owned_events_with_timeout`), returning `WithTimeout<C>`, a shared wrapper whose untimed methods use its timeout and whose explicit `*_timeout` calls override it. The traits therefore have GATs: `EventWaiter[Async]::Event<'a>` (the untimed closure's argument) and `EventIterator[Async]::Item<'a>` / `IntoEventStream::Item`: `EventRecord` for plain consumers, `EventOrTimeout` for `WithTimeout`. Generic code that needs `EventRecord` methods bounds on e.g. `for<'a> EventWaiter<Event<'a> = EventRecord<'a>>` (see the bound aliases in `shared_tests.rs`).
  - Backends implement the crate-private traits in `event_waiter::sealed` (public but unnameable, so the public traits are sealed). Every sealed method takes `timeout: Option<Duration>` and reports a timeout as `EventOrTimeout::Timeout` (`None` never times out), so one implementation serves both plain and `WithTimeout` consumers. Blanket impls derive the public traits: `Wait` → `EventWaiter`, `WaitAsync` → `EventWaiterAsync`, `Next` → `EventIterator`, `NextAsync` → `EventIteratorAsync`; `NextOwned` → `Next` (and `IntoIterator` via the shared `OwnedIter<C>`, one 6-line impl per owned type), `NextOwnedAsync` → `NextAsync` + `IntoEventStream` (`futures::stream::unfold`). Lent waiters/streams implement `Next`/`NextAsync` directly (their events borrow `self`). `WithTimeout<C>` implements the public traits from the same sealed ones with `Some(timeout)`.
  - When a closure returns `false` on a `Timeout`, owned waiters cancel as usual, and lent waiters set `cancelled` and reject (reply `E_CANCELLED` to) any event they receive afterwards: the ETW callback may already have been past its `stop_callbacks` check.
- **`EventTrace<C>`** (`consumer/event_trace.rs`): owns the consumer and the `ProcessTraceThread`, and implements each consumer trait (plus `IntoIterator` via `EventTraceIntoIter`, and `IntoEventStream`) when `C` does, by forwarding. It's a generic wrapper rather than a `dyn` object because trait objects can't conditionally implement traits and the waiter traits have generic methods. Field order matters: the consumer (or inner iterator/stream) is declared first so it's dropped—releasing any lent event—before the thread handle closes the trace. `stop_and_wait(self)` drops the consumer, closes the trace, joins, and returns ProcessTrace's result. Prefer it over hand-wiring `ProcessTraceHandle` in examples and docs.
- **Lending handoff:** the `EVENT_RECORD` pointer is only valid until the ETW callback returns, so in lent mode the callback **blocks until the consumer releases the event**. Event-returning APIs must tie the event's lifetime to a `&mut self` borrow (`fn next(&mut self) -> Option<EventRecord<'_>>`) and release the previous event at the start of the next call or on `Drop`; the borrow checker then rejects holding an event across `next()`. Never expose `Iterator`/`Stream` items or raw pointers that outlive the callback. Closure APIs (`wait_for_single_event*`) are the other sound pattern: the closure takes `EventRecord<'_>` (higher-ranked, so it can't escape) and the callback stays blocked until the closure returns (or unwinds, where a drop guard releases it). Each lending API has a `compile_fail` doctest proving this—keep them. Callers use `into_owned()` to keep events.
- **Spin before blocking on lent handoffs:** each lent event is a round trip between the ETW thread and the waiter, which usually responds within a microsecond, while blocking costs a thread sleep and wake on each side. So both sides spin briefly with exponential backoff before blocking: `lock::spin` around `try_recv` (crossbeam, flume, the futures reply), the spin phase of `Guard::wait_while` (raw, which releases the SRW lock while spinning), and `spin_poll` (futures waiter). This roughly halved lent-mode cost; keep it when changing these paths, and benchmark (steady and burst) before and after.
- Because the ETW thread is blocked while an event is lent (or while an owned-mode queue is full), callers must drain or drop the waiter/stream before joining the `ProcessTraceThread` (see the `iterate` tests).
- Consumer→ETW-thread signalling uses HRESULTs: `S_OK` continues, `E_CANCELLED` (closure returned `false`) stops the trace. Internal HRESULT constants (`S_OK`, `E_CANCELLED`, `E_TIMEOUT`, ...) live in `error.rs` as `pub(crate) const`; convert one to the public error with `.into_error()` (the crate-private `IntoError` trait).
- **Errors** are `etw_helpers::Error` (`error.rs`), a small type wrapping an `HRESULT` (`code()`, `from_hresult`, `from_win32`; implements `core::error::Error`). windows-sys functions return a raw `WIN32_ERROR`: compare with `ERROR_SUCCESS` and convert with `Error::from_win32` (`HRESULT_FROM_WIN32`; `hresult_from_win32` is public). Timeouts aren't errors (see **Timeouts**); async timeouts use `futures_timer::Delay` so they work on any executor.
- **windows-sys** types are plain data: functions take raw pointers (`PCWSTR`/`PWSTR` are `*const u16`/`*mut u16`), handles are `{ Value: u64 }` structs, and some structs lack `Default` (use `core::mem::zeroed()` or the `*_INIT` constants). `GUID` has no `PartialEq`/`Debug`: compare with `crate::test_util::guid_eq` in tests, or by `data1`..`data4`.
- Strings passed to Win32 are manually UTF-16 encoded into fixed `[u16; 1024]` buffers with a nul terminator (panics if too long). Follow this pattern rather than allocating.
- Unsafe Win32 calls go in explicit `unsafe {}` blocks even inside `unsafe fn` (edition 2024).
- `sealed::Connect::take_processor` returns `impl EventProcessor + 'static + use<>` (the trait declares `use<Self>`).
- **Profiling** uses [hotpath-rs](https://hotpath.rs) behind the opt-in `hotpath`/`hotpath-alloc` features. hotpath is an **optional dependency** (so it, and the extra flume/futures features it would enable, are absent otherwise); backend features enable its channel support with weak features (`hotpath?/flume`), so never reference `hotpath::` unconditionally.
  - Create channels with `crate::profiling::channel!(..., label = "...")` and name their types via `crate::profiling::wrap::...` (e.g. `crate::profiling::wrap::crossbeam_channel::Receiver`), which mirror hotpath's and fall back to the plain types (`profiling.rs`). Labels must be unique within the crate, or the build fails to link (`cargo check` doesn't catch it).
  - Time functions with `#[cfg_attr(feature = "hotpath", hotpath::measure(impl_type = "Type"))]` (add `future = true` on `async fn`); examples use `#[cfg_attr(feature = "hotpath", hotpath::main)]`.
  - hotpath's wrappers can't be used with `select!`-style APIs, which is why the waiters use plain `recv`/`recv_timeout`.
  - The `examples/profile_*.rs` workloads (crossbeam, flume, raw, futures, futures_stream) run a steady event stream for `PROFILE_SECONDS` (default 10) at `PROFILE_EVENTS_PER_SECOND` (default 50000) and print a hotpath report. On Windows, thread CPU is accounted in ~15.6 ms ticks, so short runs give noisy `Max%`/`Avg%`.
- Rust source files use LF line endings.
